title: Arancini

overview.description: Crisp, golden Sicilian rice balls filled with a rich ragù and melting mozzarella, coated in breadcrumbs and deep-fried. A brilliant way to use leftover risotto.

ingredients: 1 litre hot chicken or vegetable stock
method: Heat the olive oil in a large saucepan over a medium heat.
Cook the onion for 8–10 minutes until soft and translucent.
Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute.
Add the rice and stir to coat in the oil.
Pour in the wine and stir until absorbed.
Add the hot stock one ladleful at a time, stirring constantly and allowing each addition to absorb before adding the next.
Continue for 18–20 minutes until the rice is cooked but still has a little bite.
Remove from the heat and stir in the Parmesan and butter.
Season well, then spread the risotto out on a large tray to cool completely.
Refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or overnight.
To make the filling, heat the oil in a frying pan over a medium-high heat.
Add the onion and cook until softened.
Add the garlic and beef mince.
Cook, breaking up the mince, until browned.
Stir in the tomato purée and red wine.
Simmer for 10 minutes until the mixture is thick and almost dry.
Stir in the peas and season well.
Allow to cool completely.
To shape, take a small handful of cold risotto (about 70g) and flatten it in your palm.
Place a teaspoon of ragù and one or two cubes of mozzarella in the centre.
Carefully mould the rice up and around the filling, pressing firmly to form a compact ball.
Repeat with the remaining rice and filling.
Set up three shallow bowls: one with flour, one with beaten egg, and one with breadcrumbs.
Coat each arancino in flour, then egg, then breadcrumbs, pressing to adhere.
Chill the coated arancini for at least 30 minutes.
Heat the oil to 170–180°C.
Fry the arancini in batches for 3–4 minutes, turning, until deep golden brown all over.
Drain on a wire rack.
Serve immediately.

learning.did-you-know: Arancini — meaning 'little oranges' in Sicilian dialect — are one of Sicily's most iconic street foods and have been made there since at least the 10th century, when Arab rule introduced saffron and rice to the island.
learning.what-you-will-learn: How to make a proper risotto base, how to work with a moist filling without losing the shape, and how chilling is essential to achieving a crisp, well-formed croquette.

notes.why-its-in-the-chapman-kitchen: A fantastic use of leftover risotto and a genuinely crowd-pleasing snack or starter. The process teaches several important skills and produces something that freezes brilliantly.
chapman-tips: The risotto must be completely cold before shaping — warm rice will not hold together.
Keep your hands damp when shaping to prevent the rice sticking.
Press the rice firmly around the filling to avoid air pockets, which cause the arancini to burst during frying.
The filling must also be cold and dry — any excess moisture will make shaping difficult.
A second chill after breadcrumbing helps the coating set and stay intact during frying.
Don't overcrowd the fryer — the oil temperature will drop and the coating will absorb oil rather than crisp.
If the mozzarella leaks slightly, that is normal and desirable.
notes.batch-cooking: Freeze the shaped and breadcrumbed arancini on a tray in a single layer, then transfer to a freezer bag. Fry directly from frozen at a slightly lower temperature, allowing an extra 2–3 minutes cooking time.
notes.leftovers: Best eaten fresh and hot. Leftovers can be reheated in an oven or air fryer at 180°C until heated through and the coating is crisp again.
